answer.label: Not William Butler Yeats — a misattributed & reworded line
answer.sourceLine: The line traces to Eden Phillpotts's 1918 nature-vignette collection A Shadow Passes, where the original reads “The universe is full of magical things patiently waiting for our wits to grow sharper.” Over time “universe” became “world” and “wits” became “senses,” and the reworded version was then pinned on more famous names, including Yeats.

source.excerpt: The universe is full of magical things patiently waiting for our wits to grow sharper.
trail: Eden Phillpotts publishes A Shadow Passes in 1918, including the line “The universe is full of magical things patiently waiting for our wits to grow sharper,” as documented on archive.org ↗.
Over subsequent decades the wording drifts from “universe…wits” to “world…senses,” per Quote Investigator's ↗ tracing of the variant.
The reworded version begins circulating under the names of more famous writers, including William Butler Yeats and Bertrand Russell, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The Yeats attribution persists on popular quote sites today, as seen on Goodreads ↗, despite no such line appearing in Yeats's actual body of work.
source.excerptNote: The verified original line from Phillpotts's 1918 vignette, in a passage about the hidden beauty of the buckbean flower revealed under a magnifying lens — not the reworded “world…senses” version popularly credited to Yeats.
source.rightsNote: Phillpotts's original 1918 text of A Shadow Passes was published in the United States before 1931 and is in the public domain. The specific reworded “world…senses” phrasing popularly attributed to Yeats has no identified original author or publication, so its status is separately uncertain.

author.heading: About Eden Phillpotts
author.bio: Eden Phillpotts was a prolific English author best known for novels set on Dartmoor and for detective fiction such as The Red Redmaynes. He also wrote poetry and nature essays, including the 1918 collection A Shadow Passes, a series of prose-and-verse vignettes on the natural world.

misattribution.heading: Misattribution history
misattribution.intro: This is one of the more thoroughly documented cases of quote-drift: a real line by a little-remembered author, reworded and reassigned to bigger literary names.

items.why: Quote aggregators and social media widely credit Yeats with the “world…senses” wording, but Quote Investigator ↗ found no evidence Yeats wrote it, and it does not appear in his published poetry, plays, or prose.
A version closer to the original wording (“world…wits”) also circulates under Bertrand Russell's name; Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence Russell coined it either.

misattribution.truthLine: The verified original — “The universe is full of magical things patiently waiting for our wits to grow sharper” — appears in Eden Phillpotts's 1918 book A Shadow Passes, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Eden Phillpotts wrote the original line as part of a short nature vignette about the buckbean, a modest wildflower whose intricate structure only becomes visible under a magnifying lens. His point was almost scientific: better tools and sharper attention reveal hidden marvels in ordinary things — a celebration of close observation, not of mysticism.

Somewhere along the way the wording drifted. “Universe” softened into the more intimate “world,” and “wits” — a word about intellect and perception — became “senses,” nudging the line toward something more mystical and poetic. That reworded version then got attached to Yeats, whose reputation for otherworldly, fairy-haunted verse made him a plausible-sounding source even though no such line appears in his actual poems, plays, or essays.
context.pull: The universe is full of magical things patiently waiting for our wits to grow sharper. — the real, original line
